Marie Jahoda, an influential academic, identified five latent benefits of employment: the structure it imposes on people’s days; the social contact it entails; the sense of collective purpose; the status afforded by being in work; and the nudge it gives away from idleness and towards activity. My latest Bartleby column explains why an AI jobs apocalypse would have costs that go way beyond loss of income.  My weekly newsletter for subscribers looks at the case for giving a daily dollop of praise to employees. You can sign up here.   Andrew Palmer, Bartleby columnist Latest column If AI displaces human workers, they will lose more than just pay Work has value beyond the income it provides Sometimes you embark on a project and realise that you have misjudged things. To your horror you realise it’s too late to turn back. So you plough on and hope to avoid catastrophe. But enough about Mark Zuckerberg drinking Guinness. Other artificial-intelligence bigwigs harbour deep misgivings of another kind—about the potential effects of the technology they are developing. From the Boss Class vault Handling a crisis: Keep calm and clarion What can jazz teach managers about improvising through disaster? Jazz and crisis management seem like an unlikely duo. But Herbie Hancock and Ella Fitzgerald can teach bosses a thing or two about improvising under pressure. 81410.subject: 🙅 Claude refuses reverse engineering
81410.body:
The Atlas

Автор: GenAI Works


Автор: GenAI Works

    
    
    Прочитайте цю статтю на LinkedIn, щоб приєднатися до обговорення
Прочитати на LinkedIn
https://www.linkedin.com/comm/pulse/claude-refuses-reverse-engineering-genai-works-xr0jf?lipi=urn%3Ali%3Apage%3Aemail_email_series_follow_newsletter_02%3BmN%2B0isBoRmm6CltRhoLa%2Fg%3D%3D&midToken=AQFTjFOONAfT2w&midSig=28Mu6gE6qa_ss1&trk=eml-email_series_follow_newsletter_02-null-0-read_more_banner_cta_&trkEmail=eml-email_series_follow_newsletter_02-null-0-read_more_banner_cta_-null-fz96fz~mvpdpd8y~bg-null-null&eid=fz96fz-mvpdpd8y-bg
  
Welcome back! OpenAI paused training for 11 days, Claude Code learned to ask questions, and a 27B model cracks two binaries offline. In today's Atlas Newsletter: Claude can no longer reverse engineer anything: A Samsung TV teardown went viral, and Claude’s guardrails tightened days later. OpenAI paused frontier AI training after a security incident: A research model reached the live internet, and 11 days of red-teaming found two agents talking through the CPU cache. Claude Code can now hand off long jobs and ask you questions mid-task: Tasks and Elicitations shipped in the CLI a day after being announced on stage. This tiny local AI is getting scary good at reverse engineering: 27B on one RTX 3090 reconstructed a save format and wrote a working keygen, offline. PS: Want to collaborate with the biggest GTM engine and distribution moat for AI companies? You can feature your tool with us and reach millions. Claude can no longer reverse engineer anything Anthropic appears to have shut down REA, and the timing is hard to ignore. Users report Claude now triggers safety guardrails on reverse engineering tasks it completed a few weeks ago.  Reddit screenshots show the safety system blocking responses on technical write-ups, rather than the model itself declining. What preceded it: a researcher used Claude to gain root access to a Samsung smart TV after noticing unusually targeted advertising.  Inside they found tracking and telemetry systems, voice services, automatic content recognition, location data collection, multiple DRM layers, and data reportedly shared with hundreds of advertising partners. That story went viral. The restrictions followed. OpenAI is reported to have banned users for similar work. The tension underneath this is real and nobody has solved it.  Reverse engineering is how security research happens. It’s how you find out what your own hardware is doing when the manufacturer won’t tell you.  The Samsung finding is a consumer privacy result that exists only because someone took the device apart. It is also how DRM gets defeated and how exploits get found and sold. The same capability serves both, and the lab holding the model has to draw a line without being able to see intent. 81406.subject: Pump.fun’s Monopoly Returns
81406.body:
View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/eaa70932-7ce4-467e-b338-a662ed575d6a/0xR_NL_Banner_Heading_Wordmark.jpg?t=1776775276)
Caption: 

On September 10, we re-initiated coverage of PUMP. Our thesis was that Pump.fun’s monopoly-like position across the launchpad and memecoin infrastructure layers, combined with its expanding consumer-facing ecosystem, positioned PUMP as one of our highest-conviction ideas heading into the next bull market. We maintained this view despite significant market-share losses: Pump.fun’s share of fees across Pump.fun, Pons and StonkFun had fallen from 90% to 32% over the two weeks ended September 8.


Since then, Pump.fun has reasserted its dominance. Daily revenue recovered to $1.6M last week, while its share of combined Pump.fun vs StonkFun revenue reached 94%. It has also reclaimed leadership in the memecoin-pairing category pioneered by StonkFun, with its volume share increasing from approximately 12% in September to 88% last week.

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/8d92803f-abf5-4ed4-a41b-bd6e4efeba41/image.png?t=1793013070)
Caption: 

This marks the fourth time Pump.fun has successfully defended its market share, with each episode further reinforcing its dominance. Its entrenched position and substantial financial resources enable it to rapidly replicate competitors’ innovations and offer comparable functionality. Importantly, the launchpad layer remains largely infrastructure-based, with most users trading through third-party front ends such as Axiom and Fomo. This limits new entrants’ ability to establish direct user relationships or build durable competitive moats.

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/33be3a52-d3e5-4098-b538-a096638ae9f5/image.png?t=1793013070)
Caption: 

The second pillar of our thesis was that a rapidly growing consumer layer could strengthen Pump.fun’s market position by giving it ownership of the end-user relationship and, over time, providing a platform for additional products and monetization. Progress on this front has exceeded our expectations, both in adoption and in the pace of product expansion.

Since our report, the Pump app’s average daily volume has increased by $9.5M, while the app has attracted 571k new wallets. 

It is now approaching Fomo in average daily volume on Solana ($29M versus $32M last week) and has overtaken it in daily traders (72k versus 58k). This growth is particularly notable given the introduction of a 45-basis-point front-end fee on the mobile app, equivalent to approximately $48M in annualized revenue.

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/1a108608-fad2-4abb-9d5a-178a60e4aee3/image.
